questions.problem:
The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are given by

$$
A=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:y<x+3\},\,∂A=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:y=x+3\}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. The point $P(-2,1)$ lies on the boundary of $A$

II. The point $P(-2,1)$ belongs to $A$

III. The point $Q(-2,3)$ is an interior point of $A$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $\delta >0.$ A *neighborhood* of a point ${x}_{0}$ is the set of points whose distance from ${x}_{0}$ is less than $\delta .$

$$
\{x:|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta \}
$$

In two-dimensional space, a neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ is the open disc $|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta ,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14232091/assets/50a6c72e169f3104eb0b9958673cc6644f770e6bcc3ebf23360eb20189325a28.png)

Furthermore, we have the following definitions:

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is an *interior point* of a set $S$ if $S$ contains *some* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}.$ The set of all interior points of $S$ is called the *interior* of $S.$

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is a *boundary point* of a set $S$ if *every* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ contains points that are in $S$ and points that are not in $S.$ 
The set of all boundary points of $S$ is called the *boundary* of $S.$

Now, the set $A$ consists of all points that lie below the line $y=x+3.$ A sketch of this region is shown below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14232091/assets/7a23cbece856b7b842d5907665af5ea593a06faea79283b1be13fc4382e0bf26.png)

Let's add the points $P(-2,1)$ and $Q(-2,3)$ and some neighborhoods of these points to our diagram.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14232091/assets/82c921570bbc1ce700db5472871048c14c67df7d6895962f87454c70fc1ce192.png)

Let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of $P(-2,1)$ satisfy $y=x+3.$ Hence, $P$ lies in the set $∂A,$ the boundary of $A.$

- Statement II is false. The coordinates of $P(-2,1)$ do not satisfy the inequality $y<x+3.$ Hence, $P$ does not lie in the set $A.$

- Statement III is false. Indeed, $Q$ is not an interior point of $A$ since any neighborhood of $Q$ contains at least one point *outside* the set.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I only.'

questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u=4x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /12$ | $\pi /8$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\pi /3$ | $\pi /2$ |

Using the above, we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /12}^{\pi /8}3{csc}^{2}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}3{csc}^{2}⁡(u)\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(-\operatorname{cot}⁡(u))\,{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(0+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 3 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 3-\lambda  & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 6-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Since the determinant of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix is given by the product of the entries on the main diagonal, we obtain the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 3-\lambda  & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 6-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(3-\lambda )(6-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)(\lambda -3)(\lambda -6) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$

**Note:** The eigenvalues of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix are always the entries on the main diagonal.

questions.problem:
Given that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, find the least-squares solution of $Ax=b$, where 

$\,$ $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we write the given system in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}}\overset{x}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]}} & =\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}}\end{aligned}
$$

We can find the least-squares solution $\overset{^}{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{x} & =({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\  & ={([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -8\end{aligned}]\},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 9 \\ -2 & -8\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 9 \\ -2 & -8\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot (-8)-9\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}-8 & -9 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} & \frac{3}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} & \frac{3}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable $X$ is a function $F(x)$ such that

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x).
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(5) & =P(X\le 5) \\  & =P(X\in \{0,1,2,3,4,5\}) \\  & =P(X\in \{0,1,2,3\})+P(X\in \{4,5\}) \\  & =P(X\le 3)+P(3<X\le 5) \\  & =F(3)+P(3<X\le 5).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3<X\le 5) & =F(5)-F(3) \\  & =0.9997-0.9569 \\  & =0.0428.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following determinants are equal to $0?$

$$
|A|=|\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}|,\,|B|=|\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 1 & -8\end{aligned}|,\,|C|=|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -4 \\ 1 & \sqrt{5} & -2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}|
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the given determinants in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is a diagonal matrix, hence 

$$
|A|=4\cdot (-2)\cdot 3=-24\ne 0.
$$

- The matrix $B$ has a zero column: 

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 1 & -8\end{aligned}]
$$

As a result, $|B|=0.$

- The matrix $C$ has proportional columns: 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -4 \\ 1 & \sqrt{5} & -2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

As a result, $|C|=0.$

Therefore, only $|B|$ and $|C|$ are equal to $0.$
